sections.html:
New Hampshire's capital, Concord, is also the Merrimack County seat. Population is 44,597, and the city covers 67.19 square miles, so a Concord address can mean a downtown apartment, a village farmhouse or a lot on a back road. Manchester lies about 16 miles south and Boston 66 miles south.

Downtown includes the North End and South End neighborhoods, and four villages sit around it:

  • Penacook
  • Concord Heights
  • East Concord
  • West Concord

Most homes fall in the Concord School District. Penacook belongs to the Merrimack Valley School District and has a higher tax rate, as the next section shows. Interstates 89 and 93 join just south of the city limits, I-393 heads east toward the Seacoast, and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport lies 23 miles to the south. Many buyers here work for the state or the hospital, so commute and move-in timing often drive their offers.

sections.h2: Tax rate, ratio and assessing office
sections.html:
The tax year in Concord runs from April 1 through March 31. The 2025 equalization ratio is 60.4%, which means assessed values sit well below what homes sell for. Dividing a total assessed value by that ratio gives a rough market value.

2025 property tax rates by area
AreaRate per $1,000 of assessed valueSchool district
Concord (most of the city)$29.11Concord School District
Penacook$30.74Merrimack Valley School District

The last citywide update before 2026 took effect April 1, 2021. Concord then carried out a full revaluation for tax year 2026, with Vision Government Solutions doing the field and data work. Your new value may differ a lot from the old one, and the rate moves too, so do not multiply a new assessment by last year's rate to guess your bill. Late payments carry interest at 8%, prorated daily.

The assessing office is at 41 Green Street, phone 603-225-8550. Call there with questions about your property record card, square footage or the condition notes on your house.

To dispute your value, send the city an abatement application no later than March 1 after the final tax bill is issued. Abatements can be granted for good cause, usually an assessment error or a disproportionate assessment. The municipality has until July 1 to grant or deny the request. Still unhappy with the decision? Take the case to either the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, never both, with a filing deadline of September 1.

The bill stays payable while the request is pending, so pay it in full as issued. If an abatement is granted, a refund with interest follows. Saying your taxes feel high will not win a case. Back it up with comparable sales or an appraisal.

  1. Get your property record card and look for mistakes in size, age or features.
  2. Gather recent sales of similar Concord homes.
  3. Talk with the assessing office first.
  4. File the abatement application by March 1.
  5. Wait for the written answer, due by July 1.
  6. Appeal by September 1 if you still disagree.

sections.h2: What a Concord seller pays at closing
sections.html:
Under RSA 78-B, the state's real estate transfer tax is $.75 for every $100 of the sale price, and the law places it on the buyer and on the seller alike. Filing and payment go through the state's Granite Tax Connect portal. Your purchase agreement and the title company set out how the split is handled.

Expect these items on the settlement statement:

  • Transfer tax under RSA 78-B
  • Unpaid property tax for the current tax year
  • Any mortgage or lien payoff
  • Agent commission, if you list with an agent

Property tax is the other large line. The city's tax year begins April 1, so the current year's bill gets divided between you and the buyer; your closing agent will explain how. Deeds are recorded at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds, 163 N Main Street, Concord, phone (603) 228-0101. At your first meeting with the closing office, hand over a copy of your deed, the newest tax bill and a payoff request from your mortgage lender.

A seller of a one to four family home in New Hampshire has to supply a written disclosure before or while an offer is being prepared. RSA 477:4-d covers the private water supply, the private sewage system, insulation, flood hazard zone status and any underground heating oil tank.

If you do not know the answer on water, sewage or insulation, you have to say so in writing. The buyer signs to acknowledge receipt. A separate rule, RSA 477:4-c, applies before any purchase contract that includes a building. It asks for details such as the system's age, its last service date and the contractor who services it. Use the current version of the form and finish it before you accept an offer, so the contract does not stall.

Many Concord houses are old, and some still have original wiring, plaster walls or a stone foundation. Concord winters are long, cold and snowy, and inspectors know it. Expect close attention to:

  • The roof and its ability to carry a heavy snow load
  • The heating system, its age and its fuel type
  • Pipes, insulation and any sign of water intrusion
  • The foundation and drainage after spring melt

Deferred work in these areas is a common reason a financed sale stalls. An as-is cash purchase means you do not repair any of it beforehand.

A Concord house can sell while taxes are unpaid. The balance, with interest, comes out of your proceeds at closing. Before signing a contract, get a current balance from the city. The title company also needs your latest bill so the next installment lands with the correct owner.

Check the timing as well. A closing just before or just after a billing date changes who owes what for the period, and a quick conversation with your closing agent settles it. If you also owe a mortgage or a lien, the payoff letters should be ordered early.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works for a Concord house
sections.html:
In a cash sale the buyer pays directly, with no bank appraisal or underwriting to wait on. Your timeline then rests on title work and your own calendar. You describe the property, get an offer and choose whether to take it. Nothing is owed if you decline.

The transfer tax, the property tax proration and the disclosure form still apply to a cash deal. What changes is that you skip repairs, showings and the financing contingency. This suits an older house with a worn roof or aging furnace, and it suits an estate that needs a closing date it can count on.

Whatever offer you consider, pin down the closing date, the split of closing costs and what happens to any belongings left in the house.

faqs.q: Is Concord's property tax rate the same everywhere in the city?
faqs.a: No. The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000 for most of Concord and $30.74 for Penacook, which is served by the Merrimack Valley School District.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal a Concord assessment?
faqs.a: Send the abatement application by March 1 after the final tax bill. Expect the city's answer by July 1, and file any further appeal by September 1.

faqs.q: Do both the buyer and the seller pay New Hampshire's transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes, the statute imposes $.75 per $100 of the price on each of them. Your purchase agreement and title company set out who pays what at closing.

faqs.q: Does Concord have a revaluation affecting my sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Concord completed a full revaluation for tax year 2026, and the last citywide update before it took effect April 1, 2021. New values can change a buyer's tax estimate, so check your own notice.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Concord house with a private well or septic system?
faqs.a: Yes, though RSA 477:4-d requires you to hand the buyer the written water and sewage disclosure. Where you do not know an answer, write that down instead of leaving it blank.
